In summary, our research is concerned with
three main questions: (1) How did European countries perform in terms of labour markets during the Lisbon period, and, in particular, during the first phase of economic crisis?

the following questions: What can we learn about transitions from unemployment to employment and the role of ALMPs from the developments in European countries during both the Lisbon Strategy period and the economic crisis?

the following question: To what extent can we observe common trends shaped by policy learning during the Lisbon Strategy and the economic crisis and to what extent do countries remain confined to within their path dependent developments?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the countries that did better in terms of transitions from unemployment to employment during the pre crisis period, have also been able to keep unemployment low during the economic crisis, while countries that had problems in terms of transitions during the Lisbon period have also been affected by the economic crisis.

the UK and Denmark have performed better in terms of labour markets outcomes during the Lisbon period, while Germany has performed better in terms in terms of labour outcomes in the first phase the economic crisis.
the EES has had a positive impact on the European labour markets in terms of employment and unemployment, and that the economic crisis has led to a worsening of labour market outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the economic crisis has had a negative impact on employment in the EU as a group and that this impact was particularly strong in countries with high unemployment in the pre crisis situation (i.e. countries in Southern and Eastern Europe).

Denmark and Germany have done well in terms of unemployment and transitions from unemployment to employment during the Lisbon period, while the UK has done well in terms in employment, but has had a poor performance with regard to transitions from unemployment to employ ment and unemployment during the Lisbon period.
the economic crisis has not been a game changer for the labour market developments in European countries and that there is no common trend towards more active labour market policies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no clear evidence of convergence between European countries in terms of labour markets developments during the Lisbon Strategy.

the countries that have fared better during the economic crisis also performed better during the Lisbon Strategy and that the countries that fared worse during the crisis also performed worse during the Lisbon period.
